title: Selection should be evidence-based, not preference-based: Requirements, RFI/RFP, decision matrices, and contracts
overview: System selection translates organizational needs into transparent, testable criteria. This week follows the selection sequence from requirements through proposal requests and evaluation to negotiation, and examines how evidence, demonstrations, weighted scores, documented risks, contract protections, and acceptance testing support a defensible decision.
objectives: Translate organizational needs into transparent, testable system-selection criteria.
Distinguish an RFI, which explores the market, from an RFP, which requests comparable proposals.
Explain how a weighted decision matrix makes trade-offs visible while leaving judgment and decision rationale necessary.
Describe the sequence of requirements, RFP, evaluation, and negotiation.
Identify how evidence, demonstrations, documented risks, contract protections, and acceptance testing support an evidence-based system selection.

concepts.name: Evidence-based system selection
concepts.definition: Translating organizational needs into transparent, testable criteria and using requirements, comparable proposals, demonstrations, weighted scores, documented risks, contract protections, and acceptance testing.

concepts.name: Requirements
concepts.definition: Measurable criteria that translate workflow problems and organizational needs into a basis for system selection.

concepts.name: RFI
concepts.definition: A request used to explore the market.

concepts.name: RFP
concepts.definition: A request for structured, comparable vendor proposals.

concepts.name: Evaluation
concepts.definition: Scoring evidence using agreed weights and testing.

concepts.name: Negotiation
concepts.definition: The stage of selection focused on a clear contract that protects the organization.

concepts.name: Weighted decision matrix
concepts.definition: A comparison using criteria, organizational-priority weights, and evidence-based scores to make trade-offs visible; it does not replace judgment.

concepts.name: Selection judgment
concepts.definition: Human judgment and documented rationale remain necessary when interpreting a weighted comparison and making a selection decision.

concepts.name: Build
concepts.definition: An approach offering maximum control and tailored fit, with higher internal burden.

concepts.name: Buy
concepts.definition: An approach offering faster access to established features, with possible workflow mismatch.

concepts.name: Cloud
concepts.definition: An approach described as providing scalable, managed infrastructure that requires careful governance.

concepts.name: Contract clauses
concepts.definition: Clauses that should cover license, milestones, support, security, testing, and penalties.

concepts.name: Acceptance testing
concepts.definition: Testing identified as part of the evidence-based system-selection process.

concepts.name: Selection criteria
concepts.definition: Criteria shown for system comparison include workflow fit, interoperability, security, usability, support, cost, and sustainability.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities in system selection
concepts.definition: HIM connects system purpose to trustworthy information work by explaining purpose, protecting meaning and quality, supporting trust, and improving workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

concepts.name: Quality, safety, and governance principles in selection
concepts.definition: Selection principles addressing purpose and fit; data and meaning; access and trust; and workflow and adoption, supported by controls such as measurable objectives, definitions, validation, policy, role-based access, user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement.

sections.body: System selection begins by translating organizational needs and workflow problems into transparent, measurable criteria. Criteria make the basis for comparison visible rather than leaving selection to preference. The healthcare comparison in this week uses workflow fit, interoperability, security, usability, support, cost, and sustainability. These criteria connect the system's intended purpose to the work and information needs it must support.
sections.title: Turn organizational needs into testable requirements

sections.body: An RFI and an RFP serve different purposes. An RFI explores the market; an RFP asks vendors for structured, comparable proposals. Once requirements are clear, comparable responses help the organization evaluate proposals against the same stated needs. Keep the distinction focused on purpose: market exploration is not the same task as requesting comparable proposals.
sections.title: Choose the right kind of vendor request

sections.body: A weighted decision matrix makes priorities and trade-offs visible. First define criteria, then set weights to reflect organizational priorities, and score vendors using evidence and demonstrations. The matrix organizes comparison; it does not make the decision on its own. Document the rationale, risks, assumptions, and conditions so that the choice can be understood beyond the scores.
sections.title: Evaluate evidence without surrendering judgment

sections.body: The selection framework proceeds through four stages: requirements, RFP, evaluation, and negotiation. Translate workflow problems into measurable requirements; ask vendors for structured, comparable responses; score evidence using agreed weights and testing; then negotiate a clear contract to protect the organization. This sequence makes the work and points of control explicit.
sections.title: Follow the sequence from requirements to negotiation

sections.body: Selection should consider whether a system fits its intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; whether information is complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood; whether privacy, security, integrity, and auditability are protected; and whether people can use information safely and effectively. Controls described for these concerns include scope and workflow fit, definitions and validation, policy and role-based access, user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement. HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work by protecting meaning and quality, supporting appropriate access and auditability, and using feedback and testing to improve workflow.
sections.title: Protect fit, meaning, trust, and workflow

sections.body: The selection alternatives described have distinct trade-offs. Build offers maximum control and tailored fit, with higher internal burden. Buy offers faster access to established features, with possible workflow mismatch. Cloud provides scalable, managed infrastructure and requires careful governance. Whatever the approach, contract clauses should cover license, milestones, support, security, testing, and penalties. Acceptance testing is also part of an evidence-based selection, alongside demonstrations and documented risks.

activities.title: Make a defensible vendor comparison
activities.prompt: Hypothetical situation: A healthcare organization is comparing two EHR vendors. The team has criteria for workflow fit, interoperability, security, usability, support, cost, and sustainability. Which approach best supports an evidence-based selection?
activities.debrief: The selection process uses transparent criteria, agreed weights, evidence and demonstrations, and documented rationale, risks, assumptions, and conditions. A weighted matrix makes trade-offs visible but does not replace judgment.
options: Choose the vendor most preferred by the largest number of team members, without recording why.
Agree on weights reflecting organizational priorities, score evidence and demonstrations, and document rationale, risks, assumptions, and conditions.
Use cost as the only criterion and negotiate contract details after implementation.
Ask vendors for proposals with different criteria so each can emphasize its strongest areas.
